title: Build When the Customer’s Data Is Poor
subtitle: Decide whether poor warranty data can support a measurable improvement, then ship a data-repair pipeline with a small decision layer, phase by phase.
author: By Sourav Banerjee

practice_prompts.label: Opening and the decision to improve
practice_prompts.hint: Say the model-last sentence, then the clarifying questions that decide which fields matter, including whether a form or rules fix is enough.

practice_prompts.label: Measure the data and score readiness
practice_prompts.hint: Name the eight failure types with a week-one measurement each, the day-3 two-SME relabel with kappa, and your build, narrow or not-yet rule.

practice_prompts.label: Pipeline, gates and the label loop
practice_prompts.hint: Trace one claim through ingest, gates and quarantine, extraction, normalisation, the confidence router and the label store.

practice_prompts.label: Evaluation, customer and phases
practice_prompts.hint: Say what a 100-claim seed can detect, which strata you report, how you tell the customer, and each phase's exit condition.

rubric: Opened by refusing to start with model selection and tied the answer to one decision the customer wants improved.
Asked whether a rules or entry-form fix would solve the problem before proposing AI.
Split 'poor' into measurable failure types and explained why inconsistent labels are worse than missing ones.
Used chance-corrected agreement (kappa) on a two-SME relabel and read 0.81 on outcomes as usable and 0.52 on codes as not ground truth.
Stated the three-part 'not yet' condition and chose a first build, such as extraction with review, that needs no historical labels.
Put quality gates before extraction, quarantined with a reason instead of defaulting, and proposed a data contract at source.
Designed review corrections as labels: in the tool, original kept, reviewer and time recorded, disagreements adjudicated.
Sized the eval set honestly (about 11 points detectable with 200 cases at p = 0.8), split by time and reported per stratum.
Told the customer with measurements, framed phase 0 as value and wrote down the non-goals.
Exited each phase on a measured condition with shadow mode before live drafts, and answered the cost pivot with expert time as the driver.

editorial_review.evidence: Re-review against all 27 captured sections, split into 46 coverage rows. The previous version kept the tables and the 13 checks but thinned most prose: the two-minute spoken answer, two of four follow-up answers, the section 8 cost-asymmetry argument and its two quotes, the data_access_granted gate, the Snorkel/synthetic/intake quotes, the strata list, the datasheet estimate, shadow-mode definition and 11 of 15 takeaways were missing, and it misquoted '38% of claims' as new claims. I restored each, split section 8 and 11 into their own walkthrough steps (8, 9) and failure modes into its own dive, rewrote the brief around the verbatim prompt with an illustrative claim trace, added a labelled kappa example and worked sample-size arithmetic (rechecked: 1004.8 and 0.112), and replaced generic figure alt text with node-accurate text. Duplicate prose restatements of the FR/NFR tables were removed. Source inconsistencies resolved in text (2026-11-16): 'lower half' of the picture versus flowcharts that run top to bottom → the prose now describes the flowcharts as drawn (repair stages first, decision layer after), since the figures are hashed originals; 'agree about half the time beyond chance' for κ = 0.52 → the step 9 quote now says the adjusters reach about half of the agreement possible beyond chance, which is what κ = (0.52) means by its definition in step 4. November 21 complete maintained-baseline review: Complete casebook: brief and worked claim, ten walkthrough steps with every table and both figures, deep dives on labels, evaluation, failures, cost and sources, all Practice reveals, follow-ups, level calibration, the thirteen self-checks and Quick review. Targeted corrections and source-to-output mappings: /Users/sourav/Github_Repos/Forward-Deployed-Engineer-Interview-Prep/.website_spec/casebook-review-24-33-2026-11-21/build-when-customer-data-is-poor/audit.json. Historical captured-source mappings remain preserved; this pass audits the maintained baseline. Source inconsistencies settled in text (2026-11-21): Step 4 teaches that raw agreement overstates quality when one label dominates, while the phase 3 gate used raw adjuster agreement ≥ 85% → the gate keeps 85% and also reports κ and per-outcome agreement, because the case's own reasoning requires it.; Step 8 said content hashing stops duplicates looking new, while the 14% duplicates are cross-ERP records with different claim numbers → hashing catches exact re-sends only; cross-ERP matching handles the rest, because different bytes hash differently..
